title: Inhibition mechanism of the fungal β−1,3-glucan synthases by triterpenoid antifungal drugs

paper_content.introduction:
FungiareamongthemostdiversegroupsoforganismsonEarth,withan estimated over 1.5 million species1. Among them, approximately 8000speciescauseplantdiseases,andmorethan300speciescause humandiseases2. Every year, diseases related to fungal infections affectapproximately300millionpeopleworldwide,resultinginabout 1.6milliondeaths3,4. Duetothelimitedavailabilityofclinicalantifungal drugs and the continuous emergence of resistant pathogens, the expansion of the fungal infections necessitates urgent attention to developingdistincttherapeuticstrategies4–6.

β-1,3-glucansynthaseisapivotalintegralmembrane enzyme in fungal cells, catalyzing the synthesis of β-1,3-glucan, a fundamentalcomponentofthefungalcellwallthatcontributesto cell integrity and viability7,8. β-1,3-glucan synthase belongs to the glycosyltransferase48(GT48)family(http://www.cazy.org).Previous studieshavealsoshownthatRho1isessentialforactivityofthe1,3-β- glucansynthasebothinvivoandinvitro9–14. Usinguridinedi- phosphate-activated glucose (UDP-Glc) as the sugar donor, β-1,3- glucansynthasefacilitatesthecreationofβ(1→3)glycosidiclinkages in β-1,3-glucan and transports the glucan across the membrane (Fig.1a).Fungalβ-1,3-glucansynthaseisprimarilyencodedbyFKS1or FKS27.Expressionandfunctionofthetwogeneshavebeenshownto bedifferentialregulated7,15–19.InS.cerevisiae,FKS1isthepredominant isoformduringgrowth,whereasFks2isexpressedduringsporulation or under stress20. S. cerevisiae Fks1 and Fks2 share ~88% sequence identity. In S. cerevisiae, Candida albicans and many other patho- genicfungi,simultaneousknockoutofFKS1andFKS2islethal,while knockoutofFKS1aloneisalive8,21,22.MutationsinbothFks1andFks2 havebeenreportedtobeassociatedwithdrugresistance10–14.How- ever, whether Fks2 adopts a similar mechanism to Fks1 is unknownyet.

Sofar,structuresofS.cerevisiaeFks1intheapostateorincom- plexwithRho1,andanechinocandin-resistantmutantFks1(S643P)in complex with glucan product have been determined14,23,24. Among them,thecryo-EMstructureofFks1incomplexwithRho1showedthat Rho1 is positioned within a pocket between the glycosyltransferase domainofFKS1(GTdomain)andthetransmembranehelixspanning TM7–15. Structural analysis suggested Rho1’s GTP/GDP cycling may promoteadynamictransitionbetweendifferentstatesofFKS1,indu- cingtheproteinasamolecularpumptopushthegrowingglucanchain into FKS1’s transmembrane channel. However,the active sites in all availableFks1structureswerenotfullyresolved,asmanyimportant elements(such as theconservedhorizontalinterface helicesIF1/2/3 thatwereoriginallycharacterizedincellulosesynthase25)arepartially or totally invisible due to flexibility compared to the AlphaFold2 predicted model (Supplementary Fig. 1a–h). This has significantly hindered our understanding of the mechanism of β-1,3-glucan synthase.

Currently,therearetwotypesofclinicalantifungaldrugstarget- ing β-1,3-glucan synthase, including triterpenes (ibrexafungerp) and echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin, and rezafungin)22,26–29.Ibrexafungerpisasemisyntheticanalogofthenat- uraltriterpeneenfumafungin29–31.ItwasalsoanFDA(U.S.Foodand DrugAdministration)approveddruginadistinctantifungalclassfor morethan20years29.Notably,triterpeneswerehighlyactiveformany Fks1 mutant based echinocandin resistant strains, indicating its dif- ferent inhibitory mode comparing to echinocandins32–34. Despite its importance,structuralinsightsintothebindingmodeandmechanism ofthetriterpenedrugsremainunclear.

Here, we determined five different cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM)structuresofendogenousFks1andFks2intheapostate,in complex with enfumafungin, and anopen state induced by echino- candin incubation. These structures illustrate the enfumafungin binding site and an intact active site of β-1,3-glucan synthase, and depicttheconformationalchangeinducedbyechinocandinincuba- tion. Our results provide deep insights into the pharmacological mechanismsofβ-1,3-glucansynthases.

A hallmark of successful clinical management for invasive fungal disease is the availability of effective antifungal therapy, and glucan synthase inhibitors represent one of the most important drug classes. The echinocandins, approved for clinical use nearly 25 years ago, remain first-line therapy for a broad range of candidiasis and candidemia. Although they are limited to intravenous administration, they have recently been joined by the first-generation orally bioavailable enfumafungin derivatives, which also inhibit glucan synthase. Genetic studies of resistance suggest that the enfumafungin drug binds to the glucan synthase complex at a distinct yet partially overlapping site compared with the echinocandins.
Extensive knowledge has accumulated regarding the genetics, resistance mechanisms, and biochemical and kinetic properties of glucan synthase, encoded by the FKS genes. However, until recently, little was known about the enzyme’s structural organization or the molecular basis of drug–target interactions underlying inhibition—information critical for optimizing antifungal therapy. Recent cryo-EM studies from this group and others have begun to illuminate these structural features, especially concerning resistance-associated amino acid substitutions. Yet, our understanding of how echinocandins and related enfumafungin drugs achieve target inhibition remains largely inferential, based primarily on genetic analyses of resistance.
This new study by a leading glucan synthase structural biology group provides much-needed insight into the structural basis of drug–target interactions responsible for enzyme inhibition. The authors resolved five cryo-EM structures of Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, in complex with the triterpenoid enfumafungin drug, as well as in an open state induced by echinocandin drug caspofungin. Structural analysis along with strategic mutagenesis revealed the putative enfumafungin binding site, and the likely mechanism for clinically important drug-resistant mutations. Consistent with inferences from numerous genetic studies in the literature and some new mutant analysis, it is proposed that the enfumafungin attaches to transmembrane helix TM5 of the glucan synthase, reorganizes its nearby lipid environment, and stabilizes the enzyme in a unique basal state with intact active site. New insights about the location of the glucan channel, which appears to lie between TMDs 1 and 2 are exciting.
The elucidation of a structure from cryoEM studies with the enfumafungin bound is a key advancement of this work. Furthermore, the observation of an elongated extra density around the TM5 of Fks1 and Fks2 in the transmembrane region, which aligned well with the EFU molecule, was a major finding.
Overall, this is an important contribution that strongly advances the field, and supports more advanced computationally assisted drug design to develop next generation drugs that
optimize enzyme inhibition across a range of high-threat fungi and have the potential to overcome FKS hot-spot resistance known to cause refractory drug responses in patients.
Revision Considerations
The manuscript would benefit from some minor English editing:
Line 194: Hot spot 2 effect the inhibitoty function. Please correct to: Hot Spot 2 affect inhibitory function
Line 203: Should be: Therefore, it’s still unclear whether the FKS catalyze following a similar …
Line 79. ‘It indicates Fks2 may functions using a different mechanism from Fks1.’ It is well-known that FKS1 and FKS2 have different regulation and potential functon(e.g., Healey et al. 2020; Katiyar et al. 2012; Garcia-Effron et al. 2009; Gonzalez-Jimenez et al, 2025; Suwunnakorn et al. 2018)
Line 83. It suggests the regulatory subunit of Fks2 is probably Rho3. This is a helpful and insightful observation. Do we understand how Rho activates from a structural perspective?
It was reassuring to see that the enfumafungin binding site was largely overlapped with the echinocandin resistance “hot spot” regions, which aligns very well with published genetic studies, as indicated.
Lines 191-195. The potential role of a dual sterols in interacting with enfumafungin and drug resistant mutants is intriguing. However, azoles which block sterol biosynthesis and levels in the membrane are not known to have antagonistic nor synergistic effects on echinocandin nor enfumafungin action. The authors may want to speculate about this known observation.
Line 255. Did the authors look to see if caspofungin could displace or compete in enfumafungin bound density observed from the enfumafungin bound? This would get partially at the point of an overlapping binding site.
The general Discussion is sparse and should be expanded to discuss opportunities and alignment with genetic and biochemical studies. It would benefit from a description of study limitations. It is important note that in general structural resolution of 2.5–3.0 Å allows side chains to be visualized, but hydrogen positions are uncertain. For some structures at or above 3.5 Å, only backbone and bulky side chains are clear, while any atomic interactions must be inferred.
Also, the structural studies were conducted on the Saccharomyces cerevisiae glucan synthase, which is sensitive to enfumafungin but weakly sensitive to echinocandins. The authors did attempt to affirm the structural binding motifs with relevant mutant enzymes from clinically significant pathogenic Candida species, but it would be valuable to understand potentials gaps in the analysis. This particularly important in terms of interactions with sterol, bound lipids and impact on enzyme inhibition and resistance. While alpha-fold may be of limited value here, what about other computational modeling approaches? Were any energy minimizations run with bound drug for wild-type and mutant enzymes?

In this work, You and co-workers provide cryoEM structures of β-1,3-glucan synthases Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, the triterpenoid drug enfumafungin-bound state, and an open state induced by echinocandin incubation. A hallmark of successful clinical management for invasive fungal disease is the availability of effective antifungal therapy, and glucan synthase inhibitors represent one of the most important drug classes. The echinocandins, approved for clinical use nearly 25 years ago, remain first-line therapy for a broad range of candidiasis and candidemia. Although they are limited to intravenous administration, they have recently been joined by the first-generation orally bioavailable enfumafungin derivatives, which also inhibit glucan synthase. Genetic studies of resistance suggest that the enfumafungin drug binds to the glucan synthase complex at a distinct yet partially overlapping site compared with the echinocandins.
Extensive knowledge has accumulated regarding the genetics, resistance mechanisms, and biochemical and kinetic properties of glucan synthase, encoded by the FKS genes. However, until recently, little was known about the enzyme’s structural organization or the molecular basis of drug–target interactions underlying inhibition—information critical for optimizing antifungal therapy. Recent cryo-EM studies from this group and others have begun to illuminate these structural features, especially concerning resistance-associated amino acid substitutions. Yet, our understanding of how echinocandins and related enfumafungin drugs achieve target inhibition remains largely inferential, based primarily on genetic analyses of resistance.
This new study by a leading glucan synthase structural biology group provides much-needed insight into the structural basis of drug–target interactions responsible for enzyme inhibition. The authors resolved five cryo-EM structures of Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, in complex with the triterpenoid enfumafungin drug, as well as in an open state induced by echinocandin drug caspofungin. Structural analysis along with strategic mutagenesis revealed the putative enfumafungin binding site, and the likely mechanism for clinically important drug-resistant mutations. Consistent with inferences from numerous genetic studies in the literature and some new mutant analysis, it is proposed that the enfumafungin attaches to transmembrane helix TM5 of the glucan synthase, reorganizes its nearby lipid environment, and stabilizes the enzyme in a unique basal state with intact active site. New insights about the location of the glucan channel, which appears to lie between TMDs 1 and 2 are exciting.
The elucidation of a structure from cryoEM studies with the enfumafungin bound is a key advancement of this work. Furthermore, the observation of an elongated extra density around the TM5 of Fks1 and Fks2 in the transmembrane region, which aligned well with the EFU molecule, was a major finding.
Overall, this is an important contribution that strongly advances the field, and supports more advanced computationally assisted drug design to develop next generation drugs that
optimize enzyme inhibition across a range of high-threat fungi and have the potential to overcome FKS hot-spot resistance known to cause refractory drug responses in patients.

### Reviewer 2

A hallmark of successful clinical management for invasive fungal disease is the availability of effective antifungal therapy, and glucan synthase inhibitors represent one of the most important drug classes. The echinocandins, approved for clinical use nearly 25 years ago, remain first-line therapy for a broad range of candidiasis and candidemia. Although they are limited to intravenous administration, they have recently been joined by the first-generation orally bioavailable enfumafungin derivatives, which also inhibit glucan synthase. Genetic studies of resistance suggest that the enfumafungin drug binds to the glucan synthase complex at a distinct yet partially overlapping site compared with the echinocandins.
Extensive knowledge has accumulated regarding the genetics, resistance mechanisms, and biochemical and kinetic properties of glucan synthase, encoded by the FKS genes. However, until recently, little was known about the enzyme’s structural organization or the molecular basis of drug–target interactions underlying inhibition—information critical for optimizing antifungal therapy. Recent cryo-EM studies from this group and others have begun to illuminate these structural features, especially concerning resistance-associated amino acid substitutions. Yet, our understanding of how echinocandins and related enfumafungin drugs achieve target inhibition remains largely inferential, based primarily on genetic analyses of resistance.
This new study by a leading glucan synthase structural biology group provides much-needed insight into the structural basis of drug–target interactions responsible for enzyme inhibition. The authors resolved five cryo-EM structures of Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, in complex with the triterpenoid enfumafungin drug, as well as in an open state induced by echinocandin drug caspofungin. Structural analysis along with strategic mutagenesis revealed the putative enfumafungin binding site, and the likely mechanism for clinically important drug-resistant mutations. Consistent with inferences from numerous genetic studies in the literature and some new mutant analysis, it is proposed that the enfumafungin attaches to transmembrane helix TM5 of the glucan synthase, reorganizes its nearby lipid environment, and stabilizes the enzyme in a unique basal state with intact active site. New insights about the location of the glucan channel, which appears to lie between TMDs 1 and 2 are exciting.
The elucidation of a structure from cryoEM studies with the enfumafungin bound is a key advancement of this work. Furthermore, the observation of an elongated extra density around the TM5 of Fks1 and Fks2 in the transmembrane region, which aligned well with the EFU molecule, was a major finding.
Overall, this is an important contribution that strongly advances the field, and supports more advanced computationally assisted drug design to develop next generation drugs that
optimize enzyme inhibition across a range of high-threat fungi and have the potential to overcome FKS hot-spot resistance known to cause refractory drug responses in patients.

A hallmark of successful clinical management for invasive fungal disease is the
availability of effective antifungal therapy, and glucan synthase inhibitors
represent one of the most important drug classes. The echinocandins, approved
for clinical use nearly 25 years ago, remain first-line therapy for a broad range of
candidiasis and candidemia. Although they are limited to intravenous
administration, they have recently been joined by the first-generation orally
bioavailable enfumafungin derivatives, which also inhibit glucan synthase. Genetic
studies of resistance suggest that the enfumafungin drug binds to the glucan
synthase complex at a distinct yet partially overlapping site compared with the
echinocandins.
Extensive knowledge has accumulated regarding the genetics, resistance
mechanisms, and biochemical and kinetic properties of glucan synthase, encoded
by the FKS genes. However, until recently, little was known about the enzyme’s
structural organization or the molecular basis of drug–target interactions
underlying inhibition—information critical for optimizing antifungal therapy.
Recent cryo-EM studies from this group and others have begun to illuminate these
structural features, especially concerning resistance-associated amino acid
substitutions. Yet, our understanding of how echinocandins and related
enfumafungin drugs achieve target inhibition remains largely inferential, based
primarily on genetic analyses of resistance.
This new study by a leading glucan synthase structural biology group provides
much-needed insight into the structural basis of drug–target interactions
responsible for enzyme inhibition. The authors resolved five cryo-EM structures
of Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, in complex with the triterpenoid enfumafungin
drug, as well as in an open state induced by echinocandin drug caspofungin.
Structural analysis along with strategic mutagenesis revealed the putative
enfumafungin binding site, and the likely mechanism for clinically important drug-
resistant mutations. Consistent with inferences from numerous genetic studies in
the literature and some new mutant analysis, it is proposed that the enfumafungin
attaches to transmembrane helix TM5 of the glucan synthase, reorganizes its
nearby lipid environment, and stabilizes the enzyme in a unique basal state with
intact active site. New insights about the location of the glucan channel, which
appears to lie between TMDs 1 and 2 are exciting.
The elucidation of a structure from cryoEM studies with the enfumafungin bound
is a key advancement of this work. Furthermore, the observation of an elongated
extra density around the TM5 of Fks1 and Fks2 in the transmembrane region,
which aligned well with the EFU molecule, was a major finding.
Overall, this is an important contribution that strongly advances the field, and
supports more advanced computationally assisted drug design to develop next
generation drugs that
optimize enzyme inhibition across a range of high-threat fungi and have the
potential to overcome FKS hot-spot resistance known to cause refractory drug
responses in patients.

### Reviewer 2

A hallmark of successful clinical management for invasive fungal disease is the availability of effective antifungal therapy, and glucan synthase inhibitors represent one of the most important drug classes. The echinocandins, approved for clinical use nearly 25 years ago, remain first-line therapy for a broad range of candidiasis and candidemia. Although they are limited to intravenous administration, they have recently been joined by the first-generation orally bioavailable enfumafungin derivatives, which also inhibit glucan synthase. Genetic studies of resistance suggest that the enfumafungin drug binds to the glucan synthase complex at a distinct yet partially overlapping site compared with the echinocandins.
Extensive knowledge has accumulated regarding the genetics, resistance mechanisms, and biochemical and kinetic properties of glucan synthase, encoded by the FKS genes. However, until recently, little was known about the enzyme’s structural organization or the molecular basis of drug–target interactions underlying inhibition—information critical for optimizing antifungal therapy. Recent cryo-EM studies from this group and others have begun to illuminate these structural features, especially concerning resistance-associated amino acid substitutions. Yet, our understanding of how echinocandins and related enfumafungin drugs achieve target inhibition remains largely inferential, based primarily on genetic analyses of resistance.
This new study by a leading glucan synthase structural biology group provides much-needed insight into the structural basis of drug–target interactions responsible for enzyme inhibition. The authors resolved five cryo-EM structures of Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, in complex with the triterpenoid enfumafungin drug, as well as in an open state induced by echinocandin drug caspofungin. Structural analysis along with strategic mutagenesis revealed the putative enfumafungin binding site, and the likely mechanism for clinically important drug-resistant mutations. Consistent with inferences from numerous genetic studies in the literature and some new mutant analysis, it is proposed that the enfumafungin attaches to transmembrane helix TM5 of the glucan synthase, reorganizes its nearby lipid environment, and stabilizes the enzyme in a unique basal state with intact active site. New insights about the location of the glucan channel, which appears to lie between TMDs 1 and 2 are exciting.
The elucidation of a structure from cryoEM studies with the enfumafungin bound is a key advancement of this work. Furthermore, the observation of an elongated extra density around the TM5 of Fks1 and Fks2 in the transmembrane region, which aligned well with the EFU molecule, was a major finding.
Overall, this is an important contribution that strongly advances the field, and supports more advanced computationally assisted drug design to develop next generation drugs that
optimize enzyme inhibition across a range of high-threat fungi and have the potential to overcome FKS hot-spot resistance known to cause refractory drug responses in patients.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
A hallmark of successful clinical management for invasive fungal disease is the
availability of effective antifungal therapy, and glucan synthase inhibitors
represent one of the most important drug classes. The echinocandins, approved
for clinical use nearly 25 years ago, remain first-line therapy for a broad range of
candidiasis and candidemia. Although they are limited to intravenous
administration, they have recently been joined by the first-generation orally
bioavailable enfumafungin derivatives, which also inhibit glucan synthase. Genetic
studies of resistance suggest that the enfumafungin drug binds to the glucan
synthase complex at a distinct yet partially overlapping site compared with the
echinocandins.
Extensive knowledge has accumulated regarding the genetics, resistance
mechanisms, and biochemical and kinetic properties of glucan synthase, encoded
by the FKS genes. However, until recently, little was known about the enzyme’s
structural organization or the molecular basis of drug–target interactions
underlying inhibition—information critical for optimizing antifungal therapy.
Recent cryo-EM studies from this group and others have begun to illuminate these
structural features, especially concerning resistance-associated amino acid
substitutions. Yet, our understanding of how echinocandins and related
enfumafungin drugs achieve target inhibition remains largely inferential, based
primarily on genetic analyses of resistance.
This new study by a leading glucan synthase structural biology group provides
much-needed insight into the structural basis of drug–target interactions
responsible for enzyme inhibition. The authors resolved five cryo-EM structures
of Fks1 and Fks2 in the apo state, in complex with the triterpenoid enfumafungin
drug, as well as in an open state induced by echinocandin drug caspofungin.
Structural analysis along with strategic mutagenesis revealed the putative
enfumafungin binding site, and the likely mechanism for clinically important drug-
resistant mutations. Consistent with inferences from numerous genetic studies in
the literature and some new mutant analysis, it is proposed that the enfumafungin
attaches to transmembrane helix TM5 of the glucan synthase, reorganizes its
nearby lipid environment, and stabilizes the enzyme in a unique basal state with
intact active site. New insights about the location of the glucan channel, which
appears to lie between TMDs 1 and 2 are exciting.
The elucidation of a structure from cryoEM studies with the enfumafungin bound
is a key advancement of this work. Furthermore, the observation of an elongated
extra density around the TM5 of Fks1 and Fks2 in the transmembrane region,
which aligned well with the EFU molecule, was a major finding.
Overall, this is an important contribution that strongly advances the field, and
supports more advanced computationally assisted drug design to develop next
generation drugs that
optimize enzyme inhibition across a range of high-threat fungi and have the
potential to overcome FKS hot-spot resistance known to cause refractory drug
responses in patients.
